title: Polynomials
summary: This chapter connects algebra to geometry: the zeros of a polynomial are the x-coordinates of the points where its graph crosses or touches the x-axis, and a polynomial of degree n has at most n zeros. For a quadratic polynomial ax^2 + bx + c the sum of the zeros is -b/a and the product is c/a, while for a cubic ax^3 + bx^2 + cx + d the extra relation alpha beta + beta gamma + gamma alpha = c/a completes the set. These relations let you find missing coefficients, build new polynomials from given zeros and test proposed zeros by substitution. The graph of a quadratic is a parabola whose opening direction follows the sign of the leading coefficient. The division algorithm, dividend = divisor x quotient + remainder, closes the chapter and is verified in exercises with polynomials of degrees 2 and 3. Board questions concentrate on the two relations, the cubic relations and the verification step of the division algorithm.
hotTopics: Geometrical meaning of zeros as x-axis intersections
Number of zeros cannot exceed the degree
Sum and product of zeros of a quadratic polynomial
Forming a quadratic polynomial from given zeros
The three relations for a cubic polynomial
Shape of a parabola and sign of the leading coefficient

sections.heading: Polynomials Revisited: Degrees, Terms and Validity
sections.para: A polynomial in x is an expression in which the powers of x are whole numbers only: 2x^2 - 3x + 5 qualifies, while 1/x, sqrt(x) and x^(3/2) do not, because negative and fractional powers are banned. The degree is the highest power of the variable with a non-zero coefficient, and it dictates everything: a degree 1 polynomial is linear with exactly one zero, degree 2 is quadratic with at most two zeros, and degree 3 is cubic with at most three. The general forms ax^2 + bx + c with a not 0 and ax^3 + bx^2 + cx + d with a not 0 must be memorised together with their non-zero leading coefficient conditions. A constant polynomial like 7 has no zero, and the zero polynomial has every number as a zero but no defined degree.
points: Allowed powers in a polynomial are whole numbers 0, 1, 2, 3, ...; x^(-1), x^(1/2) and x^(3/2) make expressions like 1/x, sqrt(x) and x sqrt(x) non-polynomials.
Degree is the highest power with a non-zero coefficient: 4x^5 - 2x^2 + 1 has degree 5; a non-zero constant has degree 0; the degree of the zero polynomial is not defined.
Standard forms: linear ax + b, quadratic ax^2 + bx + c with a not 0, cubic ax^3 + bx^2 + cx + d with a not 0.
A polynomial of degree n has at most n zeros; a quadratic has at most 2 real zeros and a cubic at most 3.
Value at a point: for p(x) = x^2 - 3x + 2, p(2) = 4 - 6 + 2 = 0, so 2 is a zero of p(x).
Zero test: if p(k) = 0 then k is a zero of p(x), and equivalently (x - k) is a factor of p(x).
Common error: calling 2x^2 + 3/x + 1 a polynomial; the term 3/x has power -1, so the expression is not a polynomial.

keyTerms.meaning: An expression in the variable with whole-number powers only.
The highest power of the variable with a non-zero coefficient.
The coefficient of the highest power term; it must be non-zero in the standard forms.
A number k with p(k) = 0; also called a root of the equation p(x) = 0.
A polynomial of degree 0 with no zero.
The polynomial 0, for which degree is not defined and every number is a zero.

sections.trick: Whole powers only: any negative or fractional exponent makes the polynomial fake. Degree caps the zero count: degree n, at most n zeros.
sections.examPointer: One-mark questions ask which expression is not a polynomial or the maximum number of zeros of a cubic; answer 3 and quote the at-most rule, as in CBSE 2020.

sections.heading: Geometrical Meaning of Zeros: Reading Graphs
sections.para: The zero of a polynomial is where its graph meets the x-axis, because every point on the x-axis has y = 0. The graph of a linear polynomial ax + b is a straight line crossing the x-axis exactly once at x = -b/a. The graph of a quadratic ax^2 + bx + c is a parabola opening upward when a is positive and downward when a is negative; it may cut the x-axis at two points, touch it at one point or miss it entirely, matching two distinct zeros, two coincident zeros or no real zeros. Cubic graphs are S-shaped and can meet the axis one, two or three times. Counting the intersection points in a given figure is the fastest and safest way to count zeros in MCQs.
points: Zero of p(x) = the x-coordinate of any point where the graph of y = p(x) meets the x-axis; the zero is a number, not a point.
Linear ax + b with a not 0 has a straight-line graph cutting the x-axis exactly once, so it has exactly one zero.
Quadratic graphs are parabolas; a > 0 opens upward with a minimum point, a < 0 opens downward with a maximum point.
A parabola can have 2, 1 or 0 x-axis contacts: two cuts give two distinct zeros, one touch gives two coincident zeros, no contact gives no real zero.
A cubic graph always has at least one real zero and at most three; the curve may cross once, or cross and touch, giving up to three contacts.
If a figure shows the parabola cutting the x-axis at -3 and 2, the zeros are -3 and 2 and a fitting polynomial is k(x + 3)(x - 2).
The y-intercept of y = ax^2 + bx + c is c, since putting x = 0 gives y = c; the graph passes through the origin only when c = 0.

keyTerms.meaning: The U-shaped graph of a quadratic polynomial.
A point where the graph meets the x-axis; its x-coordinate is a zero.
Parabola shaped like U, which happens when a > 0.
Parabola shaped like inverted U, which happens when a < 0.
Two equal zeros produced when the parabola just touches the x-axis.

sections.trick: Count the kisses and crosses: every cross of the x-axis is a distinct zero, every touch is a repeated one; zeros can never outnumber the degree.
sections.examPointer: CBSE 2023 and CBSE 2020 both asked how many zeros the given parabola or cubic graph has; count the axis contacts in the figure, worth 1 mark.

sections.heading: Zeros and Coefficients of a Quadratic Polynomial
sections.para: For the quadratic polynomial ax^2 + bx + c with a not 0, if the zeros are alpha and beta, then two small formulas replace half the algebra of the chapter: alpha + beta = -b/a and alpha beta = c/a. They follow from the factor form a(x - alpha)(x - beta). For p(x) = 2x^2 - 7x + 3, the zeros 3 and 1/2 give the sum 7/2, which is -(-7)/2, and the product 3/2, which is c/a. The formulas work backward too: given sum 3 and product -10, the polynomial is x^2 - 3x - 10 with zeros 5 and -2. Verification by substitution should become a reflex: p(5) = 25 - 15 - 10 = 0 and p(-2) = 4 + 6 - 10 = 0 confirm the zeros.
points: Relation 1: sum of zeros alpha + beta = -b/a, that is, minus the coefficient of x over the coefficient of x^2.
Relation 2: product of zeros alpha beta = c/a, the constant term over the coefficient of x^2.
Example: 6x^2 - 7x - 3 has alpha + beta = 7/6 and alpha beta = -1/2; its actual zeros 3/2 and -1/3 confirm both.
Derivation idea: ax^2 + bx + c = a(x - alpha)(x - beta) = a(x^2 - (alpha + beta)x + alpha beta); comparing coefficients gives both formulas.
Zeros from coefficients: solve the quadratic by factorisation or the formula, then check sum and product as a quick verification.
Unknown coefficient: if one zero of kx^2 + 3x + k is 2, then 4k + 6 + k = 0, so k = -6/5; substitution is the standard trick.
More practice: if the product of zeros of x^2 - 4x + k is 5 then k = 5; if the sum of zeros of 2x^2 + kx + 6 is 5 then k = -10.

keyTerms.meaning: alpha + beta = -b/a for ax^2 + bx + c.
alpha beta = c/a for ax^2 + bx + c.
Writing the polynomial as a(x - alpha)(x - beta) using its zeros.
A constant like k found by substituting a known zero.
Substituting each zero back into the polynomial to confirm it gives 0.

sections.trick: SAP rule: Sum = -b/a, Product = c/a. The sign flips only on the sum, never on the product.
sections.examPointer: A 1 or 2 mark question gives a quadratic and asks the sum and product of its zeros (CBSE 2019, 2022); write both fractions directly and do not find the zeros unless asked.

sections.heading: Building a Quadratic from Its Zeros
sections.para: Given the zeros, constructing the polynomial is one formula: x^2 - (sum of zeros) x + product of zeros, which gives the monic polynomial with leading coefficient 1. If the zeros are 2 and -3, the polynomial is x^2 - (2 - 3)x + (2)(-3) = x^2 + x - 6, and it factors as (x - 2)(x + 3). For a general leading coefficient k, multiply the whole expression by k, and every non-zero k gives a correct answer unless the question fixes the coefficient. When the zeros are surds, such as sqrt(2) and -sqrt(2), the sum is 0 and the product is -2, so the polynomial is x^2 - 2, showing how the formula absorbs irrational zeros neatly without any separate calculation.
points: Monic reconstruction: p(x) = x^2 - (alpha + beta)x + alpha beta; the minus sign before the sum is the only trap.
Example: zeros 1/4 and -1 give sum -3/4 and product -1/4, so the polynomial is x^2 + (3/4)x - 1/4, or multiplied by 4: 4x^2 + 3x - 1.
Example: zeros 2 sqrt(3) and -2 sqrt(3) give sum 0 and product -12, so the polynomial is x^2 - 12.
Example: zeros 3 + sqrt(2) and 3 - sqrt(2) give sum 6 and product 9 - 2 = 7, so the polynomial is x^2 - 6x + 7.
With an unspecified leading coefficient, the full family is k(x^2 - (sum)x + product) for any non-zero k; boards usually accept the monic member.
Check by expansion: the polynomial from zeros 2 and -3 must expand to x^2 + x - 6, and indeed p(2) = 4 + 2 - 6 = 0.
Common error: writing x^2 + (sum)x + product; the sum enters with a minus sign only.

keyTerms.meaning: A polynomial whose leading coefficient is 1.
x^2 - (sum of zeros) x + product of zeros.
A pair like a + sqrt(b) and a - sqrt(b) whose sum and product are rational.
All non-zero multiples of a monic polynomial share the same zeros.

sections.trick: Middle sign mirrors the sum: x^2 minus (sum)x plus (product). Chant 'S goes in with a minus, P goes in with a plus'.
sections.examPointer: CBSE asks: form a quadratic polynomial whose zeros are 2 + sqrt(3) and 2 - sqrt(3), or whose sum is 8 and product is 12; 2 marks, one for sum and product, one for assembly.

sections.heading: Cubic Polynomials and Three Relations
sections.para: For the cubic ax^3 + bx^2 + cx + d with zeros alpha, beta and gamma, three relations hold: alpha + beta + gamma = -b/a, alpha beta + beta gamma + gamma alpha = c/a, and alpha beta gamma = -d/a. Notice the symmetry: the sum matches the quadratic pattern, the product carries a minus because the constant term d sits at the end of an odd-degree polynomial, and the new middle relation adds products taken two at a time. For x^3 - 4x^2 + x + 6 = (x - 2)(x - 3)(x + 1), the zeros 2, 3 and -1 give sum 4, pair-sum 1 and product -6, exactly matching -b/a = 4, c/a = 1 and -d/a = -6. Writing all three formulas before substituting is the habit that earns full marks.
points: Relation A: alpha + beta + gamma = -b/a; Relation B: alpha beta + beta gamma + gamma alpha = c/a; Relation C: alpha beta gamma = -d/a.
Worked check: x^3 - 4x^2 + x + 6 = (x - 2)(x - 3)(x + 1); zeros 2, 3, -1 give sum 4, pair-sum 1, product -6, matching the three relations.
Sign alert: for odd degree the constant-term relation carries a minus; for even degree it does not.
Third-zero shortcut: if two zeros of a cubic are known, the third equals (-b/a) minus the sum of the known two.
Reciprocal trick: 1/alpha + 1/beta + 1/gamma = (alpha beta + beta gamma + gamma alpha)/(alpha beta gamma) = -c/d for the cubic ax^3 + bx^2 + cx + d.
Example: x^3 - 6x^2 + 11x - 6 = (x - 1)(x - 2)(x - 3); the product of zeros is 1 x 2 x 3 = 6 = -(-6), confirming Relation C.
Unknown coefficient example: in x^3 - 6x^2 + kx + 8, the product of zeros is -d/a = -8, whatever the value of k; to force a desired product P you set d = -P.

keyTerms.meaning: The three formulas connecting zeros alpha, beta, gamma with coefficients a, b, c, d.
alpha beta + beta gamma + gamma alpha, the sum of products taken two at a time, equal to c/a.
For a cubic, the product of zeros equals -d/a, with a minus.
Finding the remaining zero by subtracting known zeros from -b/a.

sections.trick: Slide down the letters: sum takes b, pair-sum takes c, product takes d, and d flips its sign because the degree is odd.
sections.examPointer: A 3-mark question gives a cubic and asks for all three relations, or gives two zeros and asks for the third (CBSE 2020, 2023); write all three formulas first, then substitute.

sections.heading: The Division Algorithm for Polynomials
sections.para: Just as 47 = 5 x 9 + 2 splits a number into quotient and remainder, the division algorithm for polynomials says that if p(x) and g(x) are polynomials with g(x) not the zero polynomial, then there exist unique polynomials q(x) and r(x) such that p(x) = g(x) q(x) + r(x), where either r(x) = 0 or the degree of r(x) is less than the degree of g(x). The process is long division: divide the leading terms, multiply back, subtract, bring down, and repeat. For p(x) = 3x^3 + x^2 + 2x + 5 divided by g(x) = x^2 + 2x + 1, the quotient is 3x - 5 and the remainder is 9x + 10, and multiplying back verifies the identity exactly.
points: Division algorithm statement: p(x) = g(x) q(x) + r(x) with r(x) = 0 or degree of r(x) less than degree of g(x); q(x) is the quotient and r(x) the remainder.
Long division steps: divide the leading terms, multiply the divisor by that term, subtract, bring down the next term, repeat until the leftover degree drops below the divisor's degree.
NCERT example: (3x^3 + x^2 + 2x + 5) divided by (x^2 + 2x + 1) gives quotient 3x - 5 and remainder 9x + 10.
Verification: (x^2 + 2x + 1)(3x - 5) + 9x + 10 = 3x^3 + x^2 + 2x + 5, rebuilding the dividend exactly.
When the divisor is linear x - k, the remainder equals p(k); this is the Remainder Theorem, and r = 0 exactly when k is a zero.
If one zero of a cubic is given, say 2, then (x - 2) divides the cubic, and dividing once reduces the problem to a quadratic.
Degree bookkeeping: when the remainder is not 0, degree of p = degree of g + degree of q; if r = 0 the same equation holds exactly.

keyTerms.meaning: The identity p(x) = g(x) q(x) + r(x) with the remainder of smaller degree than the divisor.
The repeated divide-multiply-subtract-bring-down process for polynomials.
The polynomial q(x) obtained in the division.
The leftover polynomial r(x) of degree less than the divisor, possibly 0.
The remainder on dividing p(x) by x - k is p(k).

sections.trick: DMSB loop: Divide, Multiply, Subtract, Bring down; stop the loop when the leftover degree dips below the divisor's degree.
sections.examPointer: A 3 or 4 mark question asks to divide one polynomial by another and verify the algorithm (CBSE 2018, 2019); the verification line g x q + r carries its own mark, so never skip it.

sections.heading: Worked Strategy: The Five Standard Question Types
sections.para: Board questions on this chapter come in five predictable shapes, and each has a fixed solution route. Type 1 asks for the sum and product of zeros of a given quadratic: read a, b, c, write -b/a and c/a, done in two lines. Type 2 gives the zeros and asks for the polynomial: compute sum and product, then assemble x^2 - (sum)x + product. Type 3 gives one zero and an unknown coefficient: substitute the zero, solve the resulting linear equation. Type 4 divides one polynomial by another and demands verification: run long division, then multiply back. Type 5 gives a cubic with two known zeros: divide by the quadratic built from the two zeros to find the linear factor, or use the three relations. Recognising the type within ten seconds saves minutes under exam pressure.
points: Type 1: for 2x^2 - 7x + 3, sum = 7/2 and product = 3/2, read directly from the coefficients.
Type 2: zeros -2 and 3 give sum 1 and product -6, so the polynomial is x^2 - x - 6.
Type 3: if one zero of x^2 + kx + 6 is 2, then 4 + 2k + 6 = 0, so k = -5.
Type 4: dividing x^3 - 3x^2 + x + 2 by x - 2 gives quotient x^2 - x - 1 and remainder 0, so 2 is a zero.
Type 5: for x^3 - 6x^2 + 11x - 6 with zeros 2 and 3, divide by (x - 2)(x - 3) = x^2 - 5x + 6 to get x - 1, so the third zero is 1.
Marks map: 1 mark for the formula, 1 for the substitution, 1 for the conclusion; write formulas even when the answer looks obvious.
Time plan: about 90 seconds per 2-marker, 4 minutes per 3-marker, and up to 7 minutes for a division algorithm question.

keyTerms.meaning: Identifying which of the five standard shapes a question belongs to.
Placing a known zero into the polynomial to find an unknown coefficient.
Using sum and product relations instead of solving the equation.
Reducing a cubic or quartic by dividing out a known factor.

sections.trick: READ the given data: zeros given? Build. Coefficients given? Extract. One zero plus unknown? Substitute. Cubic with two zeros? Divide or use relations.
sections.examPointer: CBSE 2023 asked a 2-marker on sum and product; CBSE 2019 asked a 4-marker on the division algorithm; both patterns repeat, so drill all five types until the route is automatic.

sections.heading: Graph-Based Questions and Sign Reading
sections.para: MCQs increasingly show a figure of a parabola or a cubic and ask for the number of zeros, the signs of the coefficients or a polynomial that fits. The reading rules are mechanical. Count the x-axis contacts for the zero count. For y = ax^2 + bx + c, the opening direction gives the sign of a, the y-intercept gives the sign of c, and the position of the vertex relative to the y-axis fixes the sign of b through the vertex formula x = -b/(2a). A parabola opening upward with its vertex on the right of the y-axis has a > 0 and -b/(2a) > 0, forcing b < 0. Two minutes of rules beat two minutes of guessing in every figure-based item.
points: Number of zeros equals the number of distinct x-axis intersection points shown, capped by the degree of the polynomial.
Sign of a: upward opening means a > 0, downward opening means a < 0.
Sign of c: the y-intercept; the curve crossing the y-axis above the origin gives c > 0, below gives c < 0, through the origin gives c = 0.
Sign of b: the vertex x-coordinate is -b/(2a); for an upward parabola with vertex to the right, b < 0, and with vertex to the left, b > 0.
A parabola touching the x-axis at exactly one point has two equal zeros, previewing b^2 - 4ac = 0 from Chapter 4.
A cubic crossing the axis once has one real zero; for Class 10 only the count of visible contacts matters.
If zeros -2 and 3 are marked, the fitting monic quadratic is (x + 2)(x - 3) = x^2 - x - 6, scaled by k if the y-intercept demands it.

keyTerms.meaning: Any crossing or touching of the x-axis by the graph.
The turning point of a parabola with x-coordinate -b/(2a).
The value c at which the graph meets the y-axis.
Deducing the signs of a, b and c from the picture.

sections.trick: SAC order for signs: A from the opening, C from the y-cut, B from the vertex side. Never read b first; it is the sneakiest sign.
sections.examPointer: Figure-based MCQs appeared in CBSE 2022 and 2023; expect one item per paper on zeros from a graph, worth 1 mark, with distractors swapping touches and cuts.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes and Exam Traps
sections.para: The chapter is short, so the traps are concentrated. Students call 1/x + 2 a polynomial, forget that a quadratic has at most two real zeros, or flip the wrong sign when rebuilding a polynomial. In the division algorithm the classic losses are stopping one step early, misaligning powers during subtraction and skipping the verification line. In the cubic relations, the product sign -d/a versus d/a causes half of all errors. Write the sign rule beside every computation until it becomes automatic, and finish every long division with a substitution check at one easy value of x; a two-line check that catches most slips is worth more than a page of confident algebra.
points: Trap: x^2 + 1/x or sqrt(x) + 3 called polynomials; negative and fractional powers disqualify them.
Trap: rebuilding with x^2 + (sum)x + product; the sum term must enter with a minus sign.
Trap: writing alpha beta gamma = d/a for a cubic; the correct relation is alpha beta gamma = -d/a.
Trap: subtracting incompletely in long division so a middle term survives; write every power column, including zero coefficients.
Trap: claiming a quadratic always has two zeros; it has at most two real zeros and may have none.
Trap: giving the family k(x^2 - sx + p) when the question fixes a leading coefficient; reread the question before finalising.
Trap: skipping the verification of the division algorithm; the verification usually carries a dedicated mark.

keyTerms.meaning: The minus that appears before the sum in reconstruction and before d in the cubic product relation.
A long-division mistake caused by placing terms in wrong power columns.
The final check g(x) q(x) + r(x) = p(x) demanded by the algorithm.

sections.trick: Two minuses of Chapter 2: minus before the sum, minus before the cubic product. Chant 'sum minus, product plus, cubic product minus' before every answer.
sections.examPointer: The CBSE 2020 examiner report notes that writing the three relations before substituting prevents the -d/a slip, the most common error in this chapter.

mcqs.question: The zeros of the polynomial x^2 - 2x - 8 are
mcqs.explanation: x^2 - 2x - 8 = (x - 4)(x + 2), so the zeros are 4 and -2; sum 2 = -(-2)/1 and product -8 confirm the relations.

mcqs.question: The sum of the zeros of 2x^2 + 5x + 3 is
mcqs.explanation: Sum of zeros = -b/a = -5/2; no need to find the zeros at all.

mcqs.question: The product of the zeros of 3x^2 - 5x + 2 is
mcqs.explanation: Product of zeros = c/a = 2/3; the sign never flips for the product.

mcqs.question: If one zero of the polynomial x^2 + 3x + k is 2, then k equals
The graph of y = p(x) cuts the x-axis at exactly 3 points. The number of zeros of p(x) is
mcqs.explanation: Each x-axis intersection corresponds to one zero, so 3 contacts give 3 zeros.

mcqs.question: The maximum number of zeros that a cubic polynomial can have is
mcqs.explanation: A polynomial of degree n has at most n zeros, so a cubic has at most 3.

mcqs.question: Which of the following is NOT a polynomial?
mcqs.explanation: The term 1/x has power -1, which is not a whole number, so x^2 + 1/x is not a polynomial.

mcqs.question: If alpha and beta are the zeros of x^2 - 5x + 6, then alpha^2 + beta^2 equals
mcqs.explanation: alpha + beta = 5 and alpha beta = 6, so alpha^2 + beta^2 = (alpha + beta)^2 - 2 alpha beta = 25 - 12 = 13.

mcqs.question: A quadratic polynomial whose zeros are 2 + sqrt(3) and 2 - sqrt(3) is
mcqs.explanation: Sum = 4 and product = 4 - 3 = 1, so the polynomial is x^2 - 4x + 1.

In the division algorithm p(x) = g(x) q(x) + r(x), the degree of the remainder r(x) must be
options: less than the degree of g(x)
greater than the degree of g(x)
equal to the degree of g(x)
mcqs.explanation: The algorithm demands r(x) = 0 or degree of r(x) strictly less than the degree of g(x); otherwise the division is not complete.

mcqs.question: On dividing x^2 - 5x + 6 by x - 3, the quotient is
mcqs.explanation: x^2 - 5x + 6 = (x - 3)(x - 2), so the quotient is x - 2 and the remainder is 0.

mcqs.question: If two zeros of x^3 - 6x^2 + 11x - 6 are 1 and 2, then the third zero is
mcqs.explanation: Sum of zeros = -b/a = 6; the third zero = 6 - (1 + 2) = 3, and indeed the cubic factors as (x - 1)(x - 2)(x - 3).

mcqs.question: For the cubic polynomial x^3 - 4x^2 + x + 6, the product of its zeros equals
mcqs.explanation: For ax^3 + bx^2 + cx + d, product of zeros = -d/a = -6/1 = -6.

mcqs.question: The polynomial whose zeros are -5 and 3 is
mcqs.explanation: Sum = -5 + 3 = -2 and product = -15, so the polynomial is x^2 - (-2)x + (-15) = x^2 + 2x - 15.

mcqs.question: If one zero of the quadratic polynomial f(x) = 4x^2 - 8kx - 9 is the negative of the other, then k equals
mcqs.explanation: If the zeros are alpha and -alpha, their sum is 0, and sum = -b/a = 8k/4 = 2k, so 2k = 0 and k = 0.

mcqs.question: If alpha and beta are the zeros of x^2 - 2x + 3, then alpha^2 beta + alpha beta^2 equals
mcqs.explanation: alpha^2 beta + alpha beta^2 = alpha beta (alpha + beta). Here alpha + beta = 2 and alpha beta = 3, so the value is 3 x 2 = 6.

mcqs.question: The number of distinct quadratic polynomials having zeros -3 and 4 with no other restriction is
mcqs.explanation: Every non-zero multiple k(x + 3)(x - 4) has the same two zeros, and k can be any non-zero real number, so there are infinitely many such polynomials.

boardQuestions.question: Find the sum and the product of the zeros of the polynomial 2x^2 - 5x + 3, and verify them by finding the zeros.
boardQuestions.answer: Here a = 2, b = -5, c = 3. Sum of zeros = -b/a = 5/2 and product of zeros = c/a = 3/2. Verification: 2x^2 - 5x + 3 = 2x^2 - 2x - 3x + 3 = 2x(x - 1) - 3(x - 1) = (x - 1)(2x - 3), so the zeros are 1 and 3/2. Their sum is 1 + 3/2 = 5/2 and their product is 1 x 3/2 = 3/2, matching the values obtained from the relations.

boardQuestions.question: If alpha and beta are the zeros of the polynomial x^2 - 6x + 4, find the value of alpha^2 + beta^2.
boardQuestions.answer: From the relations, alpha + beta = -b/a = 6 and alpha beta = c/a = 4. Now use the identity alpha^2 + beta^2 = (alpha + beta)^2 - 2 alpha beta. Substituting: alpha^2 + beta^2 = 6^2 - 2 x 4 = 36 - 8 = 28. Hence alpha^2 + beta^2 = 28. The key step is to express the required expression in terms of the sum and product rather than solving for the zeros, since the zeros 3 + sqrt(5) and 3 - sqrt(5) are irrational and need not be written at all.

boardQuestions.question: Form a quadratic polynomial whose zeros are 3 + sqrt(5) and 3 - sqrt(5).
boardQuestions.answer: Let alpha = 3 + sqrt(5) and beta = 3 - sqrt(5). Sum of zeros: alpha + beta = (3 + sqrt(5)) + (3 - sqrt(5)) = 6. Product of zeros: alpha beta = (3 + sqrt(5))(3 - sqrt(5)) = 3^2 - (sqrt(5))^2 = 9 - 5 = 4. The required quadratic polynomial is x^2 - (sum)x + product = x^2 - 6x + 4. Check: x^2 - 6x + 4 = 0 has roots (6 +/- sqrt(36 - 16))/2 = (6 +/- 2 sqrt(5))/2 = 3 +/- sqrt(5), which are exactly the given zeros.

boardQuestions.question: If two zeros of the polynomial x^3 - 4x^2 + x + 6 are 2 and 3, find all the zeros of the polynomial.
boardQuestions.answer: Since 2 and 3 are zeros, (x - 2) and (x - 3) are factors, so (x - 2)(x - 3) = x^2 - 5x + 6 divides the cubic. Divide x^3 - 4x^2 + x + 6 by x^2 - 5x + 6 by long division. Step 1: x^3 divided by x^2 gives x; multiply back: x(x^2 - 5x + 6) = x^3 - 5x^2 + 6x; subtract: (x^3 - 4x^2 + x + 6) - (x^3 - 5x^2 + 6x) = x^2 - 5x + 6. Step 2: x^2 divided by x^2 gives 1; multiply back: x^2 - 5x + 6; subtract: remainder 0. So the quotient is x + 1, and the cubic = (x^2 - 5x + 6)(x + 1). Setting the quotient to 0 gives x + 1 = 0, so the third zero is -1. Hence all the zeros are 2, 3 and -1. Verification by the relations: sum = 2 + 3 - 1 = 4 = -b/a; pairwise sum = 6 - 3 - 2 = 1 = c/a; product = 2 x 3 x (-1) = -6 = -d/a. All three match the coefficients, so the answer is confirmed.

boardQuestions.question: Divide the polynomial 3x^3 + x^2 + 2x + 5 by the polynomial 1 + 2x + x^2 and verify the division algorithm.
boardQuestions.answer: Rewrite the divisor in standard form: x^2 + 2x + 1. Long division: Step 1, divide 3x^3 by x^2 to get 3x; multiply 3x(x^2 + 2x + 1) = 3x^3 + 6x^2 + 3x; subtract from 3x^3 + x^2 + 2x + 5 to get -5x^2 - x + 5. Step 2, divide -5x^2 by x^2 to get -5; multiply -5(x^2 + 2x + 1) = -5x^2 - 10x - 5; subtract to get (-x + 10x) + (5 + 5) = 9x + 10. The degree of 9x + 10 is 1, less than 2, so the division stops. Quotient q(x) = 3x - 5 and remainder r(x) = 9x + 10. Verification: (x^2 + 2x + 1)(3x - 5) = 3x^3 + 6x^2 + 3x - 5x^2 - 10x - 5 = 3x^3 + x^2 - 7x - 5; adding r(x) = 9x + 10 gives 3x^3 + x^2 + 2x + 5, which is exactly the dividend. Hence p(x) = g(x) q(x) + r(x) is verified.

boardQuestions.question: If alpha and beta are the zeros of the polynomial x^2 - 5x + k such that alpha - beta = 1, find the value of k.
boardQuestions.answer: From the relations, alpha + beta = 5 and alpha beta = k. Use the identity (alpha - beta)^2 = (alpha + beta)^2 - 4 alpha beta. Substituting the given difference: 1^2 = 5^2 - 4k, so 1 = 25 - 4k, giving 4k = 24 and k = 6. Check: for x^2 - 5x + 6 = (x - 2)(x - 3), the zeros are 3 and 2, whose difference is 1 and product is 6, confirming k = 6.

boardQuestions.question: Find the zero of the linear polynomial 5x - 7 and state the general rule for the zero of a linear polynomial ax + b.
boardQuestions.answer: The zero of a linear polynomial ax + b, with a not 0, is x = -b/a, because the graph of y = ax + b meets the x-axis exactly at x = -b/a. For 5x - 7, the zero is x = 7/5. Check by substitution: 5 x (7/5) - 7 = 7 - 7 = 0, so 7/5 is indeed the zero.

boardQuestions.question: The graph of a quadratic polynomial y = p(x) models the height of a ball thrown upward; it cuts the x-axis at x = 1 and x = 3 and the y-axis at y = 3. Answer: (i) the zeros of p(x), (ii) a quadratic polynomial fitting the data, (iii) the sum and product of the zeros.
boardQuestions.answer: (i) The zeros of p(x) are the x-coordinates of the points where the graph meets the x-axis, so the zeros are 1 and 3. (ii) A polynomial with zeros 1 and 3 has sum 4 and product 3, so the monic member is x^2 - 4x + 3. Because the y-intercept is 3, putting x = 0 in x^2 - 4x + 3 gives 3, which matches the data, so the monic polynomial itself fits: p(x) = x^2 - 4x + 3. (iii) Sum of zeros = 4 = -b/a and product of zeros = 3 = c/a, consistent with the coefficients read from p(x). Since the coefficient of x^2 is positive, the parabola opens upward, as expected for a model that returns to the ground at both ends.

boardQuestions.question: On dividing x^3 - 3x^2 + x + 2 by a polynomial g(x), the quotient and remainder were x - 2 and -2x + 4 respectively. Find g(x).
boardQuestions.answer: By the division algorithm, p(x) = g(x) q(x) + r(x), so g(x) = (p(x) - r(x))/q(x). Compute p(x) - r(x) = (x^3 - 3x^2 + x + 2) - (-2x + 4) = x^3 - 3x^2 + 3x - 2. Now divide x^3 - 3x^2 + 3x - 2 by x - 2: x^3/(x) = x^2; multiply back x^2(x - 2) = x^3 - 2x^2; subtract to get -x^2 + 3x - 2; divide -x^2 by x to get -x; multiply -x(x - 2) = -x^2 + 2x; subtract to get x - 2; divide x by x to get 1; multiply 1(x - 2) = x - 2; subtract to get remainder 0. So the quotient is x^2 - x + 1 with remainder 0, hence g(x) = x^2 - x + 1. Check: (x - 2)(x^2 - x + 1) + (-2x + 4) = x^3 - 3x^2 + 3x - 2 - 2x + 4 = x^3 - 3x^2 + x + 2, the original dividend.
